newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana plans more coffee but investors remain wary.
newsitem.headline: Ghana plans more coffee but investors remain wary.

text.p: Ghana aims to raise annual coffee production fivefold to 30,000 tonnes by 2002 with help from donors, but a stronger economy is needed to attract other investors, a World Bank official told Reuters.
"The good robusta growing areas in Ghana are as good as those in Uganda and Cameroon. There is tremendous potential for growth," World Bank agriculture specialist Robert Epworth said.
"But nobody is going to invest if inflation and subsequently interest rates are not brought down," he added.
Ghana produced around 6,000 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96, compared with Uganda's 240,000 tonnes and Cameroon's 60,000.
Epworth said the World Bank was considering granting 18 months of funding for Ghana's coffee expansion plan, but the amount had not been decided.
Ghana liberalised coffee marketing and privatised key coffee plantations in 1992 but one plantation buyer told Reuters that rehabilitation work had since been slow.
"Finance is a big problem," said a manager for Kumasi-based Goldcrest Commodities. "Interest rates are high and bureaucracy is slow."
Goldcrest bought Ghana's Otoka Farms plantations, totalling 1,400 hectares, and renamed them Plantation Resources Limited.
"So far we succeeded in rehabilitating 150 hectares," Plantation Resources manager Andy Akoto said. "We are now waiting for one year for the approval of a loan by the Agricultural Development Bank."
The International Finance Corporation (IFC), is also looking at Ghana's coffee sector and considering financing the rehabilitation of three of Goldcrest's plantations, an IFC official told Reuters.
"Hopefully in-depth appraisal will start soon," said IFC spokesman Mills Lamptey.
"The reality is that with all this good potential, growth will depend on improving the macro-economic situation," said Epworth.
Farmers began showing more interest in coffee when world market prices for coffee picked up from around 1995.
"In Ghana coffee is the poor cousin to cocoa. Growing coffee is much more work than cocoa." said Robert Epworth. "So, while the prices were low, farmers were not interested,"
